summary: Hacker News was the only platform I could read directly today, so every source below is a verbatim HN comment or thread title. The strongest themes: surprise AI/cloud bills and leaked API keys with no hard caps, small businesses squeezed by Facebook's two-links-a-month limit, Plex refugees finding Jellyfin hard to share with family, and small-site owners scrambling after a critical PHP vulnerability.

ideas.title: HardCap: a spend-capped proxy for AI and cloud API keys
ideas.oneLiner: Put your real OpenAI/Gemini/Anthropic keys behind a tiny gateway that hands out virtual keys with hard daily and monthly dollar limits.
ideas.problem: Developers keep getting surprise four-figure bills from leaked or abused keys because cloud budgets only alert and never stop spend, and a leaked or compromised vendor key has no blast-radius limit. People want per-key budgets without trusting a heavyweight gateway that itself just had a supply-chain compromise.
ideas.targetUsers: Indie developers, hackathon builders and small teams calling LLM APIs from scripts, apps and coding agents.
ideas.monetization: Free self-hosted single binary; hosted version at $9/month per project with Slack/Telegram alerts, or $29/month for teams.
mvp: Virtual keys mapped to the real provider key, injected server-side so the real key never leaves the proxy
Hard per-key daily and monthly USD caps that return 429 once exceeded
OpenAI-compatible and Gemini-compatible passthrough with token-based cost estimation
Instant kill switch and one-click key rotation
Telegram/email alert at 50/80/100% of budget
Single static binary plus Docker image

competitors.name: LiteLLM
competitors.gap: Does routing and budgets but is a large Python surface; HN users are looking for alternatives after a second PyPI compromise.

competitors.name: OpenRouter
competitors.gap: Credit-based limits only apply to OpenRouter, not to your existing Google or Anthropic keys.

competitors.name: Google Cloud budget alerts
competitors.gap: Reported as alert-only with delays of hours, so they do not stop a runaway key.

sources.title: Ask HN: My Gemini bill shot up suddenly to 2500 USD in one day
sources.quote: Unlimited billing is the main reason I will never sign up to use Google or Amazon cloud services, as I use them for other things I wouldn't want to lose access to in the event of chargebacks, etc. Cloud services signup terms are basically legal authorization for them to monetarily charge you for the result of someone else running a script. It would be very easy for these companies to implement settings for hard financial limits, but yet they refuse.

ideas.title: LinkSlot: schedule Facebook Page posts and auto-move links to the first comment
ideas.oneLiner: A scheduler that tracks your Page's free-link quota and automatically posts the link in the first comment instead of the post body.
ideas.problem: Meta is limiting professional Pages to two organic link posts a month unless they pay for Meta Verified. Small businesses, local papers and venues still rely on Facebook to reach followers and feel pushed to pay for something that used to be free.
ideas.targetUsers: Small businesses, local news outlets, venues and community organisers who post links from a Facebook Page.
ideas.monetization: Free for 1 Page with 10 scheduled posts a month; $7/month for 3 Pages and unlimited posts; $19/month for agencies.
mvp: Facebook login and Page picker via Graph API
Composer that detects links and offers: post as-is, or text-only post with the link in the first comment
Counter showing how many free link posts remain this month
Scheduling queue with preview
Optional parallel post to a free landing page or WhatsApp channel
Verify through a test Page that comment links really are not counted before launch

competitors.name: Meta Business Suite
competitors.gap: Native scheduler, but it does not manage the link quota or move links for you.

competitors.name: Buffer
competitors.gap: General cross-poster; no Facebook link-limit logic that I could find (verify before building).

competitors.name: Hootsuite
competitors.gap: Priced for agencies and enterprise rather than a local shop owner.

ideas.title: FamilyReel: invite and onboarding portal for Jellyfin libraries
ideas.oneLiner: Email invites, password self-reset and per-device setup guides that let non-technical relatives watch your Jellyfin library.
ideas.problem: People leaving Plex after its player-team layoffs find Jellyfin hard to share with family: there is no easy invite flow, remote access is a hurdle, and non-technical users struggle with clients and consoles.
ideas.targetUsers: Home-media self-hosters who share a library with parents, siblings and friends.
ideas.monetization: Free self-hosted core; $4/month hosted add-on with invite emails, branded landing page and Tailscale-style tunnel setup; $29 one-time licence for the self-hosted pro pack.
mvp: Invite by email that creates the Jellyfin user via its API
Self-service password reset page
Per-device setup cards (Apple TV, Fire TV, Android TV, Xbox, browser) with QR codes
Request-to-add-title form for family members
Health check that tells the owner why a relative cannot connect (DNS, port, certificate)
Simple admin view of who has accepted

competitors.name: Jellyfin
competitors.gap: No built-in email invite flow; remote access and family onboarding are left to the owner.

competitors.name: Plex
competitors.gap: Easier sharing, but users are leaving over ads, UI churn and the player-team layoffs.

competitors.name: Jellyseerr
competitors.gap: Handles media requests, not onboarding or connectivity troubleshooting.

ideas.title: PatchPing: plain-English alerts for small sites running vulnerable PHP
ideas.oneLiner: Enter your site URL and get an alert, with host-specific fix steps, when its PHP or WordPress stack is exposed to a newly announced critical bug.
ideas.problem: After a critical PHP RCE disclosure, small site owners do not know whether they are affected, cannot upgrade legacy PHP, and some cannot even auto-update safely. Emergency workarounds today are shell scripts.
ideas.targetUsers: Freelancers, small agencies and owners of WordPress or legacy PHP sites on shared or VPS hosting.
ideas.monetization: Free for 1 site; $5/month for 10 sites with WhatsApp/email alerts; $25/month for agencies with client reports.
mvp: Fingerprint PHP and WordPress versions from public signals
Watch advisory feeds and map them to fingerprinted sites
Alert with a plain-English verdict: affected, likely safe or cannot tell
Copy-paste mitigation per host type (cPanel, Nginx, Apache)
One-click maintenance-page snippet
Weekly digest for agencies

competitors.name: Patchstack
competitors.gap: Focused on WordPress plugin and theme vulnerabilities, not the PHP runtime itself.

competitors.name: WPScan
competitors.gap: WordPress-centric; does not help legacy non-WordPress PHP sites.

ideas.title: SubFix: fix and generate subtitles from the audio, fully offline
ideas.oneLiner: Drop in a video and an out-of-sync .srt and get it re-timed line by line using the audio, or generate subtitles when none exist.
ideas.problem: Home-media users hunt for subtitles that drift or are offset by seconds; existing fixers only shift all timestamps linearly, and people are building private scripts rather than finding a polished tool.
ideas.targetUsers: Plex/Jellyfin/Kodi users and people who watch downloaded or ripped video with external subtitles.
ideas.monetization: One-time $19 licence; free tier limited to 3 files per day.
mvp: Drag-and-drop video plus .srt
Audio-based per-line re-sync using a local speech model
Generate subtitles when none exist
Batch folder mode
Preview player with before/after timing
Writes the fixed file next to the original using media-server naming

competitors.name: alass
competitors.gap: Command-line only, which non-developers find hard to use.

competitors.name: Bazarr
competitors.gap: Downloads subtitles for the *arr stack; drift fixing is not its main job.

When I last looked for this a few years ago, I only found a really primitive one that did a linear transformation of all timestamps in the video, and none to correct each line individually.

ideas.title: KeepNumber: a real second phone number that businesses accept
ideas.oneLiner: An eSIM-backed secondary number with SMS/MMS-to-email forwarding and decent group messaging, built for people leaving Google Voice.
ideas.problem: Google Voice is stagnating, businesses increasingly reject VoIP numbers at sign-up, and group texting and SMS-to-email options are poor.
ideas.targetUsers: Freelancers, privacy-minded users and expats who keep a second number for sign-ups and client contact.
mvp: Provision a non-VoIP eSIM number through a carrier partner
Inbound SMS/MMS forwarded to email and a push notification
Group MMS support
Number port-in from Google Voice
Quiet hours and spam call screening
Per-contact labels

competitors.name: Google Voice
competitors.gap: Numbers are flagged as VoIP and feature development has stalled.

competitors.name: JMP.chat
competitors.gap: Works for some, but is VoIP-based and not seamless for non-technical users.

competitors.name: MySudo
competitors.gap: Virtual numbers can face the same VoIP rejection by verification APIs.

ideas.title: TalkText: private podcast and meeting transcripts with speaker labels
ideas.oneLiner: A drag-and-drop Mac/Windows app that turns audio into readable, speaker-labelled text with a short summary, all on-device.
ideas.problem: People want to read rather than listen and want speaker-labelled transcripts and brief summaries, but local diarization is still a hunt through model repos and they do not want their speech sent to the cloud.
ideas.targetUsers: Podcast listeners, researchers, journalists and professionals with private recordings.
ideas.monetization: One-time $29 licence, or $5/month for cloud-sync of transcripts.
mvp: Drag-and-drop audio/video file
On-device speech-to-text with speaker diarization
Rename speakers and export to Markdown/SRT/DOCX
Short summary and chapter list generated locally
Searchable library of past transcripts
Podcast RSS URL import

competitors.name: MacWhisper
competitors.gap: Mac only; speaker labelling and summaries are less central, and Windows users are not served.

ideas.title: CertWatch Lite: alert me if any CA issues a cert for my domain
ideas.oneLiner: A free-tier monitor that watches Certificate Transparency logs for your domains and pings you when an unexpected CA or issuer shows up.
ideas.problem: After a CA key compromise, domain owners realise they have no practical way to know when a rogue certificate is issued for their domain; raw CT log monitoring is heavy and rate-limited.
ideas.targetUsers: Indie developers, small SaaS owners and agencies who run their own domains.
ideas.monetization: Free for 3 domains; $5/month for 25 domains with webhook and Slack alerts; $15/month for teams.
mvp: Add domains and an allow-list of expected CAs
Poll a CT search API for new certificates
Email/Telegram alert on unexpected issuer or wildcard
Show CAA record status and suggest a fix
Weekly digest of certificates seen

competitors.name: Cert Spotter
competitors.gap: Exists, so differentiation must come from a free tier and issuer allow-list simplicity.

sources.title: eMudhra intermediate CA compromise
sources.quote: What's worse is, if this hadn't come to light, how would you even know when an attacker issues a cert for your domain? Well you might think, oh I can monitor the certificate transparency logs. I would say well, good luck downloading and parsing terabytes of certificates as they are logged.

sources.title: eMudhra intermediate CA compromise
sources.quote: Visibility through Certificate Transparency logs would at least make it a matter of record that it occurred, though.

sources.title: eMudhra intermediate CA compromise
sources.quote: Each website could try to monitor the DNS records similar to CT logs, though for targeted attacks that may not work.
